pages.name: Contractor Orientation
pages.html:
GM Only

Session 0 — Contractor Orientation

A complete GM-facing run sheet for forming the party before S01 begins.

Objective. QuestRabbit should not create the party. By the end of Session 0, QuestRabbit should be hiring a contractor team that already has history, trust, friction, unfinished business and a reason to stay together.

Recommended Running Order

TimeSectionOutcome
00:00–00:10Welcome & campaign premiseEveryone understands Brandmere, QuestRabbit and the level 1–20 campaign structure.
00:10–00:25Tone & expectationsThe group agrees the balance of comedy, danger, investigation, politics and adventuring.
00:25–00:45House rules, table policy & safetyMechanical and social expectations are explicit before characters are finalised.
00:45–01:05Company positionsPlayers understand how the official Acquisitions Incorporated franchise subsystem is being used.
01:05–01:45Character creation & concept alignmentLevel 1 concepts, ability scores, backgrounds and party suitability are settled.
01:45–02:05QuestRabbit specialist positionsEach PC chooses a distinct company position where practical.
02:05–03:00Communal backstory workshopThe team creates three shared pre-campaign jobs and their consequences.
03:00–03:25Personnel filesEach PC gains motivations, flaws, obligations, secrets and usable hooks.
03:25–03:40Relationships & practical setupAt least two PC connections each; Foundry and campaign communication confirmed.
03:40–03:50Stars & WishesImmediate calibration before S01.

If time runs short: protect the communal-history workshop. Character-sheet polish and technical questions can continue after the session; the shared past is the material that makes Session 1 feel like an established team rather than six strangers standing beside the same quest giver.

Campaign Pitch

Brandmere is a city where adventuring has been franchised. You begin as low-level independent adventurers signing with QuestRabbit Adventuring Solutions, a cheerful contractor agency with glowing job boards, corporate badges and a completely reasonable thirty-percent commission. QuestRabbit sends contractors to solve the problems fantasy corporations would rather not put in writing: missing staff, magical workplace incidents, cursed products, hostile takeovers, monsters in storerooms, franchise disputes and jobs that technically never existed.

At first, Franchise Wars is bright corporate fantasy-comedy: absurd brands, bad management, dangerous jobs and heroic people trying to survive the shift. The comedy remains, but the stakes become more serious as you discover that Brandmere's corporate structure is stranger, older and more dangerous than it looks.

Core Tone

  • The satire points upward. Owners, executives, monopolies, systems and corporate absurdity are the targets. Ordinary workers are people, not punchlines.
  • Comedy does not erase consequence. Ridiculous situations can still hurt people and change the city.
  • The party has agency. They may negotiate, refuse, expose, embarrass, help or exploit employers. They do not need to admire QuestRabbit or Corporate Row.
  • The campaign premise is still binding. Every character needs a reason to take dangerous work and a reason to keep adventuring with the team.

Character Creation Baseline

  • Starting level: 1.
  • Ability scores: Standard Array or 27-point buy. No rolled ability scores.
  • Use the table's declared player-option baseline consistently. Do not combine legacy/current versions of the same feature unless approved.
  • Normal class/background starting equipment plus one small themed trinket from the character's previous life.
  • Acquisitions Incorporated company positions sit beside class/background; they do not replace either.
  • Individual written backstories may follow Session 0. Useful unfinished business matters more than length; the existing maximum remains ten pages.

Questions to Ask the Whole Table

Campaign Mix

How much do you want of roleplay, combat, investigation, exploration, politics, puzzles, business management, horror and comedy?

Group Contract

What makes this team stay together when a contract becomes inconvenient, unprofitable or morally ugly?

Character Principle

What are you willing to sell — and what are you not willing to sell?

QuestRabbit

Why are you applying now rather than remaining completely independent?

Do Not Reveal During Session 0

  • The true meaning of Rabbit Rating.
  • The metaphysical purpose of the party's signatures.
  • Creation & Company's real position in the ownership structure.
  • The Final Contract, Clause 77-B, or the true function of Receipts.
  • The hidden mechanics of the Commons Tally.
  • The later Board vote.
  • The significance of the Franchise Below.

Players only need to know that contracts, reviews, records and reputation matter in Brandmere.

Close Checklist

  • Character concept, class, species and background confirmed.
  • Ability score method completed.
  • Company position chosen for every PC; roles unique where practical.
  • Every character has a reason to take QuestRabbit work.
  • Three communal past jobs exist.
  • At least one friendly NPC, one rival/debt and one unpaid act of kindness exist.
  • Every PC has at least two relationships with other PCs.
  • Every PC has at least one unresolved personal hook.
  • Safety additions are recorded privately.
  • Foundry access and campaign communication work.
  • Stars & Wishes have been completed.
  • No PC is built around permanently refusing the campaign premise.

After Session 0

Record character names, players, class/background/species, company positions, core motivations, flaws, hard lines, corporate temptations, important NPCs, the three shared jobs, party relationships, rival/debt, communal keepsake, safety notes and the night's Stars & Wishes. These become immediate inputs for personal side contracts and recurring NPCs.

pages.name: Orientation
pages.html:
Player Facing

Welcome to Franchise Wars

QuestRabbit contractor orientation: what this campaign is and what your character needs.

Brandmere is a city where adventuring has been franchised. Every major chain has a flagship, every holding company has a tower, and QuestRabbit Adventuring Solutions has found a way to take thirty percent of danger.

Your Starting Position

You are a level 1 adventurer joining a small contractor team. QuestRabbit does not own your character, your beliefs or your loyalty. It provides contracts, ratings, specialist credentials and access to work. What you do with those opportunities is yours.

Expect missing employees, magical workplace incidents, cursed products, hostile takeovers, monsters in storerooms, franchise disputes, corporate espionage, strange customers and jobs that technically never existed.

The Campaign

  • Levels 1–20.
  • Corporate fantasy-comedy with real consequences.
  • Combat, investigation, social manoeuvring, exploration, contracts, moral choices and recurring NPCs.
  • Characters may be ambitious, cynical, idealistic, greedy, anti-corporate, desperate, loyal or opportunistic.
  • The satire targets power and systems. Ordinary employees are people caught in those systems.

What Your Character Needs

  • A believable reason to take paid adventuring work.
  • A reason to cooperate with the other PCs.
  • At least one desire strong enough to create difficult choices.
  • At least one principle, relationship or part of themselves they do not want to sell.
  • Enough flexibility to remain part of an ensemble campaign.

Character Creation

  • Starting level: 1.
  • Ability scores: Standard Array or 27-point buy.
  • Normal class/background equipment.
  • Choose one small personal trinket connected to a former employer, family, craft, vice, ambition, failure or important relationship.
  • Your QuestRabbit company position is chosen separately from your class and background.
Orientation Question

Before QuestRabbit, I took dangerous work because…

pages.name: Mechanical House Rules
pages.html:
Player Facing

House Rules

The mechanical rules used throughout Franchise Wars.

Powerful Critical Hits

On a natural 20 attack, deal the maximum value of the attack's normal damage dice, then roll those damage dice normally and add the normal modifier once.

Natural-1 Complications

A natural 1 can create a fictionally appropriate complication that moves the scene forward. It is not an automatic slapstick failure and it is not permission for arbitrary punishment. The rule applies to PCs and NPCs.

Potions

  • Drink a potion yourself: Bonus Action.
  • Administer a potion to another creature: Action.
  • Healing potions restore their maximum listed healing.
  • Consuming more than one potion within one in-game hour triggers the established Potion Toxicity check/table.

Quick Checks in Combat

A brief observational or interpretive check may be free when it represents a quick glance or immediate read of the scene. Sustained searching, negotiation, detailed manipulation or significant multitasking can cost an Action or carry a situational penalty. The cost follows what the character is actually attempting.

Stacking Inspiration

Inspiration awards can stack. They are especially appropriate when a player commits to a trait, ideal, bond or flaw in a way that meaningfully complicates the character's life; accepts a detrimental consequence because it is right for the character; or creates strong collaborative roleplay.

Blind Death Saves

Death saves are secret/blind. The rest of the table does not know the exact success/failure count while the character is unconscious.

pages.name: Table Policy
pages.html:
Player Facing

Table Policy

The social contract for a collaborative campaign.

  • Respect people in and out of character. Personal attacks, derogatory language and belittling are not acceptable.
  • Listen when someone has the floor. Give character moments, descriptions and decisions room to land.
  • Stay engaged. Real-life interruptions happen; prolonged unrelated browsing, phone use or side conversations should not become routine.
  • Arrive ready. Have access to Foundry and know your core features well enough to take a turn without rebuilding your character at the table.
  • Keep rulings moving. Questions and respectful corrections are welcome. Once a ruling is made for the scene, move on and revisit it after the session if necessary.
  • Share spotlight. Busy social scenes can become effectively turn-based. Give everyone room to act and speak.
  • Characters can argue; players remain collaborators.
  • PvP is exceptional and consent-based. Theft from another PC, harmful magic, deliberate friendly fire or major betrayal should not be sprung on another player as a surprise.
  • Step away when needed. If it is urgent, simply go. No scene is more important than a real person.

pages.name: Safety & Feedback
pages.html:
Player Facing

Open Door, Boundaries & Feedback

Simple tools for keeping the campaign comfortable without interrupting its momentum.

Baseline Boundaries

  • Line: sexual violence.
  • Line: direct harm to children as entertainment or graphic content.
  • Line: graphic torture descriptions.
  • Veil: sexual activity fades to black.

Open Door

Anyone can say pause, say hold on, message the DM privately, or step away. No justification is required in the moment. The scene can be reframed, skipped, retconned or moved past. New boundaries can be added privately at any time.

Campaign Content

Franchise Wars can include corporate exploitation, predatory contracts, workplace mistreatment, fantasy violence, undead and monsters, magical coercion, some body-horror-adjacent magical incidents, infernal/legalistic supernatural threats, and satire of consumption, employment and wealth.

Stars & Wishes

Most sessions close with a quick calibration:

  • Star: something another player, the DM, a scene or the game did that worked well.
  • Wish: something you want more of, less of, or hope to see in future.

Wishes are forward-looking guidance for making the campaign better.

pages.name: Using Acquisitions Incorporated
pages.html:
Player Facing

QuestRabbit Specialist Positions

The official Acquisitions Incorporated franchise subsystem, re-skinned for Brandmere.

Rules Source. Use the official Acquisitions Incorporated sourcebook for the exact company-position mechanics, rank features, specialist equipment and franchise-task rules. Franchise Wars references those mechanics rather than reproducing proprietary rules text.

Each PC chooses one company position where practical. The position is an additional organisational role; it does not replace class or background.

PositionQuestRabbit FunctionCharacter Question
CartographerRoutes, mapping, travel and getting the team where the contract says it is.When did following your directions once get somebody hurt?
DecisionistVotes, group decisions, morale and resolving indecision when nobody wants responsibility.What decision do you still regret?
DocumancerContracts, records, paperwork, clauses and making bureaucracy useful before it becomes lethal.Why are you suspicious of contracts?
HoardspersonResources, loot, inventory and the uncomfortable question of who gets what.What possession could you never bring yourself to sell?
LoremongerResearch, names, history, institutional memory and facts somebody hoped had been forgotten.What secret do you already know that you should not?
ObviatorThreat analysis, tactical weaknesses and making obstacles stop being obstacles.When did destroying something make the situation worse?
OccultantDanger, death, supernatural consequence and the strange accounting of what a life costs.Why are you unusually comfortable around death?
SecretarianContacts, communications, reputation, information and making the right person hear the right version of events.When did a lie save somebody?

Franchise Wars Adaptation

  • QuestRabbit issues the specialist authority/equipment while the party operates through the Warren.
  • Position rank follows the official franchise-rank progression in the sourcebook.
  • Specialist items remain role-specific property rather than ordinary shared loot.
  • Official Franchise Tasks and Downtime can be used between contracts for research, marketing, schmoozing, headquarters work and related operations.
  • The party's early operational base is its QuestRabbit workspace at the Warren. A dedicated headquarters can develop through play.
  • The QuestRabbit thirty-percent commission represents early agency overhead. Do not also apply a second layer of low-level franchise operating costs while the party remains a QuestRabbit contractor team.
  • Rabbit Rating, Leverage, Commons Tally, Receipts, Folios and Board control are separate Franchise Wars campaign systems.

pages.name: Three Jobs Before QuestRabbit
pages.html:
Player Facing

Communal Backstory Workshop

Build the contractor team by creating the jobs they survived before the campaign began.

Opening Round

Complete the sentence: Before QuestRabbit, I took dangerous work because…

These jobs happened before S01. They are not secret campaign missions; they are the shared résumé that explains why this team already knows how to work together.

Job One — The Job We Brag About

Create one low-level contract that genuinely went well.

  1. Who hired you?
  2. What was the apparently simple job?
  3. What unexpected thing made it dangerous?
  4. Who took charge?
  5. Who did something impressive nobody else could have done?
  6. Whose mistake nearly ruined it?
  7. What ordinary person remembers you fondly because of what happened?
  8. What trophy, receipt, broken object, scar or ridiculous souvenir survived?
  9. What exaggerated version of the story do you tell strangers?

Job Two — The Job We Never Mention

Create the group's shared professional embarrassment.

  1. What did the client actually ask for?
  2. What did the party misunderstand?
  3. What was destroyed, lost, awakened, released, delivered to the wrong person or accidentally signed?
  4. Who tried to warn everyone?
  5. Who took the blame publicly?
  6. Who actually caused it?
  7. Who still has an unpaid bill, grievance or legal complaint because of it?
  8. Which rival contractor knows what really happened?
  9. What phrase causes the whole party to go quiet because of this job?

Job Three — The Job We Did for Free

Create the moment that proves what the team is like when nobody is paying.

  1. Who needed help?
  2. Why was there no money in it?
  3. Who first said yes?
  4. Who objected and then helped anyway?
  5. What promise did the party make?
  6. What did helping cost them?
  7. Which NPC, family, worker, neighbourhood, guild or small business still remembers?
  8. What small gift or keepsake did they receive instead of payment?
  9. Would they make the same choice again?

Team Formation

  • How did the characters first meet?
  • Why did they choose to take a second job together?
  • What makes each character useful to the team that has nothing to do with damage output?
  • Which two characters disagree most often, and why does that not break the group?
  • Who normally speaks to a client?
  • Who reads the fine print?
  • Who is trusted with the money?
  • Who gets blamed when there is no obvious culprit?
  • What is the party's unwritten rule?
  • Why are they applying to QuestRabbit now?

One Shared Keepsake

Choose one small object from the old days that the team keeps together. It should be small enough to sit in the eventual office and meaningful enough that losing it would hurt.

pages.name: Character-to-Character Bonds
pages.html:
Player Facing

Character-to-Character Bonds

Give every PC relationships that existed before the first campaign contract.

Go around the table. Each player answers at least two prompts involving different PCs.

  • Which character have you known longest?
  • Which character owes you money?
  • Which character knows something embarrassing about you?
  • Which character did you initially dislike but now trust?
  • Which character have you lied to?
  • Which character has seen you at your absolute worst?
  • Which character would you trust with your life but not your wallet?
  • Which character's approval secretly matters to you?
  • Which character did you once cover for?
  • Which character are you slightly jealous of?

Relationships do not need to be symmetrical. One character may believe another is their closest friend while the feeling is not fully returned.

Create One Shared NPC

Invent one ordinary person in Brandmere who already knows the team: a tavern owner, retired adventurer, street-food vendor, shopkeeper, former employer, neighbour, union representative, teacher, courier, craftsperson or similar.

Round the Table

Why does this person know your character?

pages.name: Personnel File
pages.html:
Player Facing

Contractor Personnel File

Questions designed to give the DM material that can return as real campaign consequences.

Core Personnel Questions

  1. What do you want badly enough to risk your life for money?
  2. What do you believe having enough money would actually fix?
  3. What is your relationship with authority? Obedient, cynical, rebellious, manipulative, aspirational, frightened, something else?
  4. What is the worst professional or personal failure you have had?
  5. What principle do you claim you would never compromise?
  6. What secret could seriously damage your reputation if your colleagues learned it?
  7. Who outside the party matters enough that you would abandon a contract to help them?
  8. What kind of person immediately earns your sympathy?
  9. What kind of person immediately earns your contempt?
  10. What does success look like to you right now?

Private Questions for the DM

These can be answered privately after the communal workshop.

  1. What is something your character desperately wants but should not receive easily?
  2. What unresolved relationship from their past would you enjoy seeing appear?
  3. What mistake from their past could realistically come back to hurt them?
  4. What belief would be interesting for the campaign to challenge?
  5. Is there something you would enjoy the DM revealing about your character that the other PCs initially do not know?

Quick Eight

If time is short, the DM needs at least these eight pieces:

  • What can a bad employer exploit because you want it so badly?
  • What will you not sell, betray or compromise even for life-changing money?
  • Who depends on you?
  • Who do you owe — money, loyalty, an apology or a favour?
  • What failure still influences your decisions?
  • What flaw gets worse under stress?
  • What secret would hurt your reputation if made public?
  • What would make you walk away from QuestRabbit?

pages.name: Hook Mapping
pages.html:
GM Only

DM Hook Integration

Turn Session 0 answers into recurring Franchise Wars material without exposing the campaign machinery.

Player MaterialCampaign Connections
Authority / institution traumaQuestRabbit bureaucracy, Crown & Cleaver executives, inspections, contracts, arbitration and institutional power.
Money / security / statusRaises, retainers, executive access, Hoard Syndicate wealth, Rabbit Rating perks and offers that should be genuinely tempting.
Worker sympathy / anti-exploitationUnderpaid staff, labour disputes, the Old Independents, small businesses and Marda Hobb.
Family business / craft / local rootsThe Old Independents' Quarter, the Rows, Harbour & Driftwood or another Brandmere district threatened or tempted by expansion.
Contracts / law / bureaucracyDocumancy, Arbitration Court, Guild of Scriveners, disputed clauses, Folios and recurring paperwork.
Fame / storytelling / public recognitionMcGuffin Narrative Holdings, Songbird Quarter, public reviews, Rabbit Rating publicity and corporate PR.
Planar / magical backgroundPlanar Quay, Planar Hospitality Group, strange imports and extraplanar clients.
Death / undeath / griefRestaurant Necromancy Group, Nine Circles Hospitality, undead workers and questions about personhood as an asset.
Food / hospitality / retail backgroundConnect a family, former employer or rival directly to a franchise or an independent business.
Shame / professional failureA rival contractor knows enough to needle the PC but not enough to invalidate the character.
A person they protectPlace that NPC somewhere the campaign revisits naturally. Do not default to kidnapping; let consequences reach them in varied ways.

Session 0 Deliverables to Record

  • Final character names and player names.
  • Class, background and species.
  • Company position.
  • Core motivation and core flaw.
  • Hard line the character will not cross.
  • Temptation Corporate could exploit.
  • Important NPCs and places.
  • The three shared jobs and their consequences.
  • Party relationships and communal keepsake.
  • Rival/debt.
  • Safety notes.
  • Stars & Wishes.

Use the Material Early

Do not wait until Act IV to acknowledge the backstories. Put at least one Session 0 NPC, debt, promise, rival, former employer or personal ambition into the first several contracts. The players should learn immediately that what they created matters.

pages.name: Systems
pages.html:
Campaign Systems

The campaign uses five tracking systems. None is complicated; together they make every side contract matter to the finale. Keep a single sheet—the Contractor File—on which you record all five.

Contract Grades

GradeLevelsTypical WorkBase Pay
Copper 1–4 Pest control, deliveries, missing employees, petty espionage 25–150 gp
Silver 5–8 Monster nests, sabotage, dangerous acquisitions, supernatural workplace incidents 300–1,500 gp
Gold 9–12 Interplanar procurement, corporate warfare, powerful magical entities 2,000–8,000 gp
Platinum 13–16 Demonic mergers, dimensional monopolies, ancient franchises, catastrophes 10,000–40,000 gp
Black Card 17–20 Jobs that technically never existed Payment in kind

The 30%. QuestRabbit deducts thirty per cent of every fee. Pip Ashworth will explain that this is industry standard. It is not. Players who negotiate directly with a client (Persuasion DC 15 [[/check skill=per dc=15]] + the grade's tier) can cut QuestRabbit out—but a contract taken off the board doesn't count toward the Rabbit Rating.

The Rabbit Rating

The party shares a single rating from one to five stars. It begins at one star when they sign the Contractor Agreement in S1. Publicly, it's a customer-satisfaction score that unlocks better contracts. Secretly, it measures how much ordinary people trust the party—and it is the metaphysical threshold that makes their signatures valid for the Material Plane.

StarsUnlocksHidden Meaning (DM)
★ Copper contracts; a badge Known to one neighbourhood
★★ Silver contracts; QuestRabbit expense account (50 gp/month) Trusted by a district
★★★ Gold contracts; a Folio page is opened in the party's name (S10) Trusted by a city
★★★★ Platinum contracts; a private office at the Warren Trusted by a nation
★★★★★ Black Card; an invitation to the AGM (S20) Representatives of the Commons: signature valid for the Material Plane

Earning Stars. The rating is not XP. It rises at the milestones shown in the spine (S2, S5, S10, S15 and S20 each add a star if the party completed the act's missions) and it can rise early if the party does something that makes the public love them. It never falls below the star count the spine requires—the Ledger won't allow it. Players who try to tank their rating deliberately (rudeness, sabotage, refusing jobs) discover that one-star reviews simply don't post. This is the first clue, around Act III, that the rating isn't what it seems.

The Mandate (optional). If the party cuts ties with QuestRabbit, the rating continues under a new name: the Mandate, tracked in the Folio page Wand-Mart opens for them in S10. Nothing changes except the font.

Leverage

Leverage represents dirt, debts, favours and secrets the party holds over a specific corporation. Track Leverage separately for each of the ten Board umbrellas plus Creation & Company. Every contract in this book lists a Leverage target; completing it with the truth exposed (not buried) grants 1 Leverage against that target. Spine missions grant the amounts they list.

Spending Leverage. A point can be spent at any time to gain one of the following against the target corporation, its staff or its directors:

  • Advantage. Advantage on one Charisma check, or on one argument in the Clause Debate (S24).
  • Access. A door opens: a meeting, a warehouse, a file, a board member's private dining room.
  • Cover. The corporation's security looks the other way for one scene.
  • Proxy. In S23, 2 Leverage against an umbrella lets the party demand its director's proxy. The director may refuse, but must then be dealt with in person.

Losing Leverage. Leverage is lost when the party is bought off (accepting a “bonus” from the target), when their evidence is destroyed, or when they use it and the target retaliates—at your discretion, one point spent in a heavy-handed way costs one more.

The Commons Tally

The Grand Ledger records only written agreements. Handshakes, favours done for free, gifts, promises made in a tavern and kept—these are invisible to it. Creation & Company can't see them, can't buy them and can't cancel them.

Whenever the party helps someone and refuses payment, or makes an unwritten promise and keeps it, record that person or group on the Commons Tally. Named NPCs count as one; a union, a neighbourhood or a guild counts as one. Most side contracts note where a Tally ally can be won instead of gold.

  • In play. Tally allies show up. Call on one per session for a small favour—no roll.
  • In S23. Tally allies attend the Extraordinary General Meeting as observers. For every five, one wavering director has disadvantage to refuse the party.
  • In S24. Each Tally ally present can act as a witness. Clauses with no Receipt can be voided by three witnesses in place of a DC 25 argument. The Held in Common ending requires at least twenty.

Receipts

A Receipt is proof. Twelve spine missions each produce one specific Receipt that voids one clause of the Final Contract; a thirteenth (Incident Report 77-B) is found in the first hour of the campaign and voids the clause that makes the party signatories. Other missions produce Receipts that weaken Tallis Vend or open the way forward.

Receipts are physical. Put them on index cards and hand them to the players. Lose track of one and it's gone; destroyed Receipts can be reconstructed only by a DC 25 argument or three Tally witnesses. By level 20 the players should have a stack of cards they've been carrying for a year, and should suddenly understand why.

Folios

A Folio is a branch ledger: a lesser book that synchronises with the Grand Ledger. Every major corporation keeps them. Entries written in a Folio become true within that corporation's holdings. The party's first Folio is found in S10 (Wand-Mart); see Appendix B for the magic item. Folios are how the party learns the rules of the Ledger before they ever see it—and how you can dramatise “paperwork is reality” at every level.

The Board

Creation & Company rules through a Board of ten directors, one per umbrella corporation, plus the Chairman. Tallis Vend controls 51% through their proxies. In S23, the party needs six seats flipped (the director votes against Vend) or removed (the director is gone and their proxy void). Each umbrella's dossier in Chapter 5 lists exactly how its seat turns. Track the Board on the Contractor File from S8 onward; the players should be able to see the vote coming for two whole acts.
